entries.745523affa9f7e2760dbfab14fa95cd1c7fc3b7c: <div sID="gen4776" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Judg.7" sID="Judg.7"/> <div eID="gen4776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4777" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4778" type="x-p"/> This chapter presents us with Gideon in the field, commanding the army of Israel, and routing the army of the Midianites, for which great exploit we found in the former chapter how he was prepared by his converse with God and his conquest of Baal. We are here told, I. What direction God gave to Gideon for the modelling of his army, by which it was reduced to 300 men, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.8">8</reference>. II. What encouragement God gave to Gideon to attack the enemy, by sending him secretly into their camp to hear a Midianite tell his dream, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.9-Judg.7.15">ver. 9-15</reference>. III. How he formed his attack upon the enemy's camp with his 300 men, not to fight them, but to frighten them, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.16-Judg.7.20">ver. 16-20</reference>. IV. The success of this attack; it put them to flight, and gave them a total rout, the disbanded forces, and their other neighbours, then coming in to his assistance, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.21-Judg.7.25">ver. 21-25</reference>. It is a story that shines very brightly in the book of the wars of the Lord.
entries.ffa9fe68c8061f1149d51fbc23421cca39f2c380: <div eID="gen4778" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4777" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Gideon's Three Hundred Men. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4779" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Jerubbaal, who <hi type="italic">is</hi> Gideon, and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, rose up early, and pitched beside the well of Harod: so that the host of the Midianites were on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Gideon, The people that <hi type="italic">are</hi> with thee <hi type="italic">are</hi> too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever <hi type="italic">is</hi> fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Gideon, The people <hi type="italic">are</hi> yet <hi type="italic">too</hi> many; bring them down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there: and it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> of whom I say unto thee, This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee; and of whomsoever I say unto thee, This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go. <hi type="super">5</hi> So he brought down the people unto the water: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Gideon, Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself; likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the number of them that lapped, <hi type="italic">putting</hi> their hand to their mouth, were three hundred men: but all the rest of the people bowed down upon their knees to drink water. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the <hi type="italic">other</hi> people go every man unto his place. <hi type="super">8</hi> So the people took victuals in their hand, and their trumpets: and he sent all <hi type="italic">the rest of</hi> Israel every man unto his tent, and retained those three hundred men: and the host of Midian was beneath him in the valley. <div eID="gen4779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4780" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Gideon applies himself with all possible care and industry to do the part of a good general, in leading on the hosts of Israel against the Midianites (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He rose up early,</hi> as one whose heart was upon his business, and who was afraid of losing time. Now that he is sure God is with him he is impatient of delay. He pitched near a famous well, that his army might not be distressed for want of water, and gained the higher ground, which possibly might be some advantage to him, for the Midianites <hi type="italic">were beneath him in the valley.</hi> Note, Faith in God's promises must not slacken, but rather quicken, our endeavours. When we are sure God goes before us, then we must bestir ourselves, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.24">2 Sam. v. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen4780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4781" type="x-p"/> II. God provides that the praise of the intended victory may be reserved wholly to himself, by appointing 300 men only to be employed in this service. <div eID="gen4781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4782" type="x-p"/> 1. The army consisted of 32,000 men, a small army in comparison with what the Midianites had now brought into the field; Gideon was ready to think them too few, but God comes to him, and tells him they are <hi type="italic">too many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.2">v. 2</reference>. Not but that those did well who offered themselves willingly to this expedition, but God saw fit not to make use of all that came. We often find God bringing great things to pass by a few hands, but this was the only time that he purposely made them fewer. Had Deborah lately blamed those who <hi type="italic">came not to the help of the Lord,</hi> and yet in the next great action must those be turned off that do come? Yes; (1.) God would hereby show that when he employed suitable instruments in his service he did not need them, but could do his work without them, so that he was not indebted to them for their service, but they to him for employing them. (2.) He would hereby put those to shame for their cowardice who had tamely submitted to the Midianites, and durst not make head against them, because of the disproportion of their numbers. They now saw that, if they had but made sure of the favour of God, one of them might have chased a thousand. (3.) He would hereby silence and exclude boasting. This is the reason here given by him who knows the pride that is in men's hearts: <hi type="italic">Lest Israel vaunt themselves against me.</hi> Justly were those denied the honour of the success. <hi type="italic">My own hand hath saved me</hi> is a word that must never come out of the mouth of such as shall be saved. <hi type="italic">He that glories must glory in the Lord,</hi> and all flesh must be silent before him. <div eID="gen4782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4783" type="x-p"/> 2. Two ways God took to lessen their numbers:—(1.) He ordered all that would own themselves timorous and faint-hearted to be dismissed, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.3">v. 3</reference>. They were now encamped on a mountain close to the enemy, called <hi type="italic">Mount Gilead,</hi> from Gilead, the common ancestor of these families of Manasseh, which were seated on this side Jordan (<reference osisRef="Num.26.30">Num. xxvi. 30</reference>), and thence they might see perhaps the vast numbers of the enemy; those therefore who were disheartened at the sight were left to their liberty, to go back if they pleased. There was a law for making such a proclamation as this, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.8">Deut. xx. 8</reference>. But Gideon perhaps thought that concerned only those wars which were undertaken for the enlarging of their coast, not, as this, for their necessary defence against an invader; therefore Gideon would not have proclaimed this if God, who knew how his forces would hereby be diminished, had not commanded him. Cowards would be as likely as any, after the victory, to take the honour of it from God, and therefore God would not do them the honour to employ them in it. One would have thought there would be scarcely one Israelite to be found that against such an enemy as the Midianites, and under such a leader as Gideon, would own himself fearful; yet above two parts of three took advantage of this proclamation, and filed off, when they saw the strength of the enemy and their own weakness, not considering the assurances of the divine presence which their general had received of the Lord, and, it is likely, delivered unto them. Some think the oppression they had been under so long had broken their spirits, others, more probably, that consciousness of their own guilt had deprived them of their courage. Sin stared them in the face, and therefore they durst not look death in the face. Note, Fearful faint-hearted people are not fit to be employed for God; and, among those that are enlisted under the banner of Christ, there are more such than we think there are. (2.) He directed the cashiering of all that remained except 300 men, and he did it by a sign: <hi type="italic">The people are yet too many</hi> for me to make use off, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.4">v. 4</reference>. See how much God's thoughts and ways are above ours. Gideon himself, it is likely, thought they were too few, though they were as many as Barak encountered Sisera with (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.14">ch. iv. 14</reference>); and, had he not forced his way through the discouragement by dint of faith, he himself would have started back from so hazardous an enterprise, and have made the best of his own way back. But God saith, they are <hi type="italic">too many,</hi> and, when diminished to a third part, they are yet <hi type="italic">too many,</hi> which may help us to understand those providences which sometimes seem to weaken the church and its interests: its friends are too many, too mighty, too wise, for God to work deliverance by; God is taking a course to lessen them, that he may be <hi type="italic">exalted in his own strength.</hi> Gideon is ordered to bring his soldiers to the watering, probably to the well of Harod (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">v. 1</reference>) and the stream that ran from it; he, or some appointed by him, must observe how they drank. We must suppose they were all thirsty, and were inclined to drink; it is likely he told them they must prepare to enter upon action immediately, and therefore must refresh themselves accordingly, not expecting, after this, to drink any thing else but the blood of their enemies. Now some, and no doubt the most, would kneel down on their knees to drink, and put their mouths to the water as horses do, and so they might get their full draught. Others, it may be, would not make such a formal business of it, but as a dog laps with his tongue, a lap and away, so they would hastily take up a little water in their hands, and cool their mouths with that, and be gone. Three hundred and no more there were of this latter sort, that drank in haste, and by those God tells Gideon he would rout the Midianites, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.7">v. 7</reference>. By the former distinction none were retained but hearty men, that were resolved to do their utmost for retrieving the liberties of Israel; but by this further distinction it was provided that none should be made use of but, [1.] Men that were hardy, that could endure long fatigue, without complaining of thirst or weariness, that had not in them any dregs either of sloth or luxury. [2.] Men that were hasty, that thought it long till they were engaged with the enemy, preferring the service of God and their country before their necessary refreshment; such as these God chooses to employ, that are not only well affected, but zealously affected in a good thing. And also because these were the smaller number, and therefore the least likely to effect what they were designed for, God would by them save Israel. It was a great trial to the faith and courage of Gideon, when God bade him let all the rest of the people but these 300 <hi type="italic">go every man to his place,</hi> that is, go where they pleased out of his call, and from under his command; yet we may suppose those that were hearty in the cause, though now set aside, did not go so far out of hearing but that they were ready to follow the blow, when the 300 had broken the ice, though this does not appear. Thus strangely was Gideon's army purged, and modelled, and reduced, instead of being recruited, as one would think in so great an action it both needed and deserved to be. Now, <div eID="gen4783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4784" type="x-p"/> 3. Let us see how this little despicable regiment, on which the stress of the action must lie, was accoutred and fitted out. Had these 300 been double-manned with servants and attendants, and double-armed with swords and spears, we should have thought them the more likely to bring something to pass. But, instead of making them more serviceable by their equipment, they are made less so. For, (1.) Every soldier turns butler: They <hi type="italic">took victuals in their hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.8">v. 8</reference>), left their bag and baggage behind, and every man burdened himself with his own provision, which was a trial of their faith, whether they could trust God when they had no more provisions with them than they could carry, and a trial of their diligence, whether they would carry as much as they had occasion for. This was indeed living from hand to mouth. (2.) Every soldier turns trumpeter. The regiments that were cashiered left their trumpets behind them for the use of these 300 men, who were furnished with these instead of weapons of war, as if they had been going rather to a game than to a battle.
entries.37ccc9d910c76fea884d49579071773c98a4ffff: <div eID="gen4784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4785" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And it came to pass the same night, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Arise, get thee down unto the host; for I have delivered it into thine hand. <hi type="super">10</hi> But if thou fear to go down, go thou with Phurah thy servant down to the host: <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou shalt hear what they say; and afterward shall thine hands be strengthened to go down unto the host. Then went he down with Phurah his servant unto the outside of the armed men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the host. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like grasshoppers for multitude; and their camels <hi type="italic">were</hi> without number, as the sand by the sea side for multitude. <hi type="super">13</hi> And when Gideon was come, behold, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a man that told a dream unto his fellow, and said, Behold, I dreamed a dream, and, lo, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian, and came unto a tent, and smote it that it fell, and overturned it, that the tent lay along. <hi type="super">14</hi> And his fellow answered and said, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> nothing else save the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel: <hi type="italic">for</hi> into his hand hath God delivered Midian, and all the host. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it was <hi type="italic">so,</hi> when Gideon heard the telling of the dream, and the interpretation thereof, that he worshipped, and returned into the host of Israel, and said, Arise; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian. <div eID="gen4785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4786" type="x-p"/> Gideon's army being diminished as we have found it was, he must either fight by faith or not at all; God therefore here provides recruits for his faith, instead of recruits for his forces. <div eID="gen4786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4787" type="x-p"/> I. He furnishes him with a good foundation to build his faith upon. Nothing but a word from God will be a footing for faith. He has this as full and express as he can desire, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.9">v. 9</reference>. 1. A word of command to warrant the action, which otherwise seemed rash and indiscreet, and unbecoming a wise general: <hi type="italic">Arise, get thee down</hi> with this handful of men <hi type="italic">unto the host.</hi> 2. A word of promise to assure him of the success, which otherwise seemed very improbable: <hi type="italic">I have delivered it into thy hand;</hi> it is all thy own. This <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> came to him the same night, when he was (we may suppose) greatly agitated and full of care how he should come off; <hi type="italic">in the multitude of his thoughts within him these comforts did delight his soul.</hi> Divine consolations are given in to believers not only strongly but seasonably. <div eID="gen4787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4788" type="x-p"/> II. He furnishes him with a good prop to support his faith with. 1. He orders him to be his own spy, and now in the dead of the night to go down privately into the host of Midian, and see what intelligence he could gain: "<hi type="italic">If thou fear to go down</hi> to fight, go first only with thy own servant (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.10">v. 10</reference>) and <hi type="italic">hear what they say</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.11">v. 11</reference>); and it is intimated to him that he should hear that which would greatly strengthen his faith. God knows the infirmities of his people, and what great encouragement they may sometimes take from a small matter; and therefore, knowing beforehand what would occur to Gideon, in that very part of the camp to which he would go down, he orders him to go down and hearken to what they said, that he might the more firmly believe what God said. He must take with him <hi type="italic">Phurah his servant,</hi> one that he could confide in, probably one of the ten that had helped him to break down the altar of Baal. He must take him and no one else with him, must take him with him to be a witness of what he should hear the Midianites say, that out of the mouth of these two witnesses, when the matter came to be reported to Israel, the word might be established. He must take his servant with him, because two are better than one and a little help is better than none. 2. Being so, he orders him the sight of something that was discouraging. It was enough to frighten him to discern, perhaps by moon-light, the vast numbers of the enemy (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.12">v. 12</reference>), the men like grasshoppers for multitude, and they proved no better than grasshoppers for strength and courage; the camels one could not count, any more than the sand. But, 3. He causes him to hear that which was to him a very good omen; and when he had heard it he went back again immediately, supposing he now had what he was sent thither for. He overheard two soldiers of the enemy, that were comrades, talking; probably they were in bed together, waking in the night. (1.) One of them tells his dream, and as our dreams generally are, and therefore not worth telling again, it is a very foolish one. He dreamed that he saw a barley-cake come rolling down the hill into the camp of the Midianites, and "methought," says he (for so we speak in telling our dreams), "this rolling cake struck one of our tents" (perhaps one of the chief of their tents) "and with such violence that" (would you think it?) "it overturned the tent, forced down the stakes, and broke the cords at one blow, so that the tent lay along and buried its inhabitants," <reference osisRef="Judg.7.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">In multitudes of dreams there are divers vanities,</hi> says Solomon, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Eccl. v. 7</reference>. One would wonder what odd incoherent things are often put together by a ludicrous fancy in our dreams. (2.) The other, it may be between sleeping and waking, undertakes to interpret this dream, and the interpretation is very far-fetched: <hi type="italic">This is nothing else save the sword of Gideon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.14">v. 14</reference>. Our expositors now can tell us how apt the resemblance was, that Gideon, who had threshed corn for his family, and made cakes for his friend (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.11-Judg.6.19">ch. vi. 11-19</reference>), was fitly represented by a cake,—that he and his army were as inconsiderable as a cake made of a little flour, as contemptible as a barley-cake, hastily got together as a cake suddenly baked upon the coals, and as unlikely to conquer this great army as a cake to overthrow a tent. But, after all, do <hi type="italic">not interpretations belong to God?</hi> He put it into the head of the one to dream and into the mouth of the other to give the sense of it; if Gideon had heard the dream only, and he and his servant had been left to interpret it themselves, it had so little significancy in it that it would have done him little service; but, having the interpretation from the mouth of an enemy, it not only appeared to come from God, who has all men's hearts and tongues in his hand, but it was likewise an evidence that the enemy was quite dispirited, and that the name of Gideon had become so formidable to them that it disturbed their sleep. The victory would easily be won which was already so tamely yielded: <hi type="italic">Into his hand hath God delivered Midian.</hi> Those were not likely to fight who saw God fighting against them. <div eID="gen4788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Gideon, observing the finger of God pointing him to this very place, at this very time, to hear this dream and the interpretation of it, was exceedingly encouraged by it against the melancholy apprehensions he had upon the reducing of his army. He was very well pleased to hear himself compared to a barley-cake, when it proved to effect such great things. Being hereby animated, we are told (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.15">v. 15</reference>), 1. How he gave God the glory of it; he worshipped immediately, bowed his head, or, it may be, lifted up his eyes and hands, and in a short ejaculation thanked God for the victory he was now sure of, and for this encouragement to expect it. Wherever we are, we may speak to God, and worship him, and find a way open heavenward. God must have the praise of that which is encouraging to our faith, and his providence must be acknowledged in those events which, though minute and seemingly accidental, prove serviceable to us. 2. How he gave his friends a share in the encouragements he had received: <hi type="italic">Arise,</hi> prepare to march presently; <hi type="italic">the Lord has delivered Midian into your hand.</hi>
entries.af83f130a522f419d479cdd8cef929a003c05dc3: <div eID="gen4789" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Midianites Surprised. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4790" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And he divided the three hundred men <hi type="italic">into</hi> three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise: and, behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be <hi type="italic">that,</hi> as I do, so shall ye do. <hi type="super">18</hi> When I blow with a trumpet, I and all that <hi type="italic">are</hi> with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and say, <hi type="italic">The sword</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and of Gideon. <hi type="super">19</hi> So Gideon, and the hundred men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in their hands. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow <hi type="italic">withal:</hi> and they cried, The sword of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and of Gideon. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they stood every man in his place round about the camp: and all the host ran, and cried, and fled. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Beth-shittah in Zererath, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to the border of Abel-meholah, unto Tabbath. <div eID="gen4790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4791" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The alarm which Gideon gave to the hosts of Midian in the dead time of the night; for it was intended that those who had so long been a terror to Israel, and had so often frightened them, should themselves be routed and ruined purely by terror. <div eID="gen4791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4792" type="x-p"/> 1. The attack here made was, in many circumstances, like that which Abraham made upon the army that had taken Lot captive. The number of men was much the same: Abraham had 318, Gideon 300; they both divided their forces, both made their attack by night, and were both victorious under great disadvantages (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.14-Gen.14.15">Gen. xiv. 14, 15</reference>); and Gideon is not only a son of Abraham (so were the Midianites by Keturah) but an heir of his faith. Gideon, (1.) Divided his army, small as it was, into three battalions (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.16">v. 16</reference>), one of which he himself commanded (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.19">v. 19</reference>), because great armies (and such a one he would make a show of) were usually divided into the right wing, and left wing, and the body of the army. (2.) He ordered them all to do as he did, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.17">v. 17</reference>. He told them now, it is very likely, what they must do, else the thing was so strange that they would scarcely have done it of a sudden, but he would, by doing it first, give notice to them when to do it, as officers exercise their soldiers with the word of command or by beat of drum: <hi type="italic">Look on me, and do likewise.</hi> Such is the word of command which our Lord Jesus, the captain of our salvation, gives his soldiers; for he has <hi type="italic">left us an example,</hi> with a charge to follow it: <hi type="italic">As I do, so shall you do.</hi> (3.) He made his descent in the night, when they were secure and least expected it, which would put them into great consternation, and when the smallness of his army would not be discovered. In the night all frights are most frightful, especially in the dead of the night, as this was, a little after midnight, when the middle watch began, and the alarm would wake them out of their sleep. We read of <hi type="italic">terror by night</hi> as very terrible (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.5">Ps. xci. 5</reference>), and <hi type="italic">fear in the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.8">Cant. iii. 8</reference>. (4.) That which Gideon aimed at was to frighten this huge host, to give them not only a fatal rout, but a very shameful one. He accoutred his army with every man a trumpet in his right hand, and an earthen pitcher, with a torch in it, in his left, and he himself thought it no disparagement to him to march before them thus armed. He would make but a jest of conquering this army, and goes out against them rather as against a company of children than against a host of soldiers. <hi type="italic">The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">laughed thee to scorn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>. The fewness of his men favoured his design; for, being so few, they marched to the camp with the greater secresy and expedition, so that they were not discovered till they were close by the camp; and he contrived to give the alarm when they had just mounted the guards (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.19">v. 19</reference>), that the sentinels, being then wakeful, might the sooner disperse the alarm through the camp, which was the best service they could do him. Three ways Gideon contrived to strike a terror upon this army, and so put them into confusion. [1.] With a great noise. Every man must blow his trumpet in the most terrible manner he could and clatter an earthen pitcher to pieces at the same time; probably each dashed his pitcher to his next man's, and so they were broken both together, which would not only make a great crash, but was a figure of what would be the effects of the fright, even the Midianites' killing one another. [2.] With a great blaze. The lighted torches were hid in the pitchers, like <hi type="italic">a candle under a bushel,</hi> until they came to the camp, and then, being taken out all together of a sudden, would make a glaring show, and run through the camp like a flash of lightning. Perhaps with these they set some of the tents on the outside of the camp on fire, which would very much increase the confusion. [3.] With a great shout. Every man must cry, <hi type="italic">For the Lord, and for Gideon,</hi> so some think it should be read in <reference osisRef="Judg.7.18">v. 18</reference>, for there the sword is not in the original, but it is in <reference osisRef="Judg.7.20">v. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.</hi> It should seem, he borrowed the word from the Midianite's dream (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.14">v. 14</reference>): it is <hi type="italic">the sword of Gideon.</hi> Finding his name was a terror to them, he thus improves it against them, but prefixes the name of Jehovah, as the figure without which his own was but an insignificant cypher. This would put life into his own men, who might well take courage when they had such a God as Jehovah, and such a man as Gideon, both to <hi type="italic">fight for,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">fight for them;</hi> well might those follow who had such leaders. It would likewise put their enemies into a fright, who had of old heard of Jehovah's great name, and of late of Gideon's. The sword of the Lord is all in all to the success of the sword of Gideon, yet the sword of Gideon must be employed. Men the instruments, and God the principal agent, must both be considered in their places, but men, the greatest and best, always in subserviency and subordination to God. This army was to be defeated purely by terrors, and these are especially the <hi type="italic">sword of the Lord.</hi> These soldiers, if they had swords by their sides, that was all, they had none in their hands, but they gained the victory by shouting "The sword." So the church's enemies are routed by <hi type="italic">a sword out of the mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.21">Rev. xix. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen4792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4793" type="x-p"/> 2. This method here taken of defeating the Midianites may be alluded to, (1.) As typifying the destruction of the devil's kingdom in the world by the preaching of the everlasting gospel, the sounding of that trumpet, and the holding forth of that light out of earthen vessels, for such the ministers of the gospel are, in whom the treasure of that light is deposited, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6, 7</reference>. Thus God chose the <hi type="italic">foolish things of the world to confound the wise,</hi> a barley-cake to overthrow the tents of Midian, that the <hi type="italic">excellency of the power might be of God only;</hi> the gospel is a sword, not in the hand, but in the mouth, the sword <hi type="italic">of the Lord and of Gideon,</hi> of God and Jesus Christ, him that sits on the throne and the Lamb. (2.) As representing the terrors of the great day. So the excellent bishop Hall applies it; if these pitchers, trumpets, and firebrands, did so daunt and dismay the proud troops of Midian and Amalek, who shall be able to stand before the last terror, when the trumpet of the archangel shall sound, the elements shall be on a flame, the heavens pass away with a great noise, and the Lord himself shall descend with a shout! <div eID="gen4793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4794" type="x-p"/> II. The wonderful success of this alarm. The Midianites were shouted out of their lives, as the walls of Jericho were shouted down, that Gideon might see what he lately despaired of ever seeing, the <hi type="italic">wonders that their fathers told them of.</hi> Gideon's soldiers observed their orders, and <hi type="italic">stood every man in his place round about the camp</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.21">v. 21</reference>), sounding his trumpet to excite them to fight one another, and holding out his torch to light them to their ruin. They did not rush into the host of Midian, as greedy either of blood or spoil, but patiently stood still to <hi type="italic">see the salvation of the Lord,</hi> a salvation purely of his own working. Observe how the design took effect. 1. They feared the Israelites. <hi type="italic">All the host</hi> immediately took the alarm; it flew like lightning through all their lines, and <hi type="italic">they ran, and cried, and fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.21">v. 21</reference>. There was something natural in this fright. We may suppose they had not had intelligence of the great diminution of Gideon's army, but rather concluded that since their last advices it had been growing greater and greater; and therefore they had reason to suspect, knowing how odious and grievous they had made themselves and what bold steps had been taken towards the throwing off of their yoke, that it was a very great army which was to be ushered in with all those trumpeters and torch-bearers. But there was more of a supernatural power impressing this terror upon them. God himself gave it the setting on, to show how that promise should have been fulfilled if they had not forfeited it, <hi type="italic">One of you shall chase a thousand.</hi> See the power of imagination, and how much it may become a terror at some times, as at other times it is a pleasure. 2. They fell foul upon one another: <hi type="italic">The Lord set every man's sword against his fellow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">v. 22</reference>. In this confusion, observing the trumpeters and torch-bearers to stand still without their camp, they concluded the body of the army had already entered and was in the midst of them, and therefore every one ran at the next he met, though a friend, supposing him an enemy, and one such mistake as this would occasion many, for then he that slew him would certainly be taken for an enemy, and would be dispatched immediately. It is our interest to preserve such a command of our own spirits as never to <hi type="italic">be afraid with any amazement,</hi> for we cannot conceive what mischiefs we thereby plunge ourselves into. See also how God often makes the enemies of his church instruments to destroy one another; it is a pity the church's friends should ever be thus infatuated. 3. They fled for their lives. Perhaps when day-light came they were sensible of their mistake in fighting with one another, and concluded that by this fatal error they had so weakened themselves that now it was impossible to make any head against Israel, and therefore made the best of their way towards their own country, though, for aught that appears, the 300 men kept their ground. <hi type="italic">The wicked flee when none pursueth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Terrors make him afraid on every side, and drive him to his feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job xviii. 11</reference>.
entries.3846e91b9ca652f66e84e48250ed1ba823182c63: <div eID="gen4794" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Gideon's Victory. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4795" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And the men of Israel gathered themselves together out of Naphtali, and out of Asher, and out of all Manasseh, and pursued after the Midianites. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Gideon sent messengers throughout all mount Ephraim, saying, Come down against the Midianites, and take before them the waters unto Beth-barah and Jordan. Then all the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together, and took the waters unto Beth-barah and Jordan. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; and they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb, and pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side Jordan. <div eID="gen4795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4796" type="x-p"/> We have here the prosecution of this glorious victory. 1. Gideon's soldiers that had been dismissed, and perhaps had begun to disperse themselves, upon notice of the enemies' flight got together again, and vigorously pursued those whom they had not courage to face. The men of Israel out of Naphtali and Asher who did this (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.23">v. 23</reference>) were not such as now came from those distant countries, but the same that had enlisted themselves (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.35">ch. vi. 35</reference>), but had been cashiered. Those who were fearful and afraid to fight (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.3">v. 3</reference>) now took heart, when the worst was over, and were ready enough to divide the spoil, though backward to make the onset. Those also that might not fight though they had a mind to it, and were disbanded by order from God, did not as those, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.10">2 Chron. xxv. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">13</reference>, <hi type="italic">return in great anger,</hi> but waited for an opportunity of doing service in pursuing the victory, though they were denied the honour of helping to force the lines. 2. The Ephraimites, upon a summons from Gideon, came in unanimously, and secured the passes over Jordan, by the several fords, to cut off the enemies' retreat into their own country, that they might be entirely destroyed, to prevent the like mischief to Israel another time. Now that they had begun to fall, it was easy to say, Down with them, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.13">Esth. vi. 13</reference>. They <hi type="italic">took the waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.24">v. 24</reference>), that is, posted themselves along the river side, so that the Midianites, who fled from those who pursued them, fell into the hands of those that waited to intercept them. Here were <hi type="italic">fear, and the pit, and the snare,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17">Isa. xxiv. 17</reference>. 3. Two of the chief commanders of the host of Midian were taken and slain by the Ephraimites on this side Jordan, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">v. 25</reference>. Their names perhaps signified their nature, <hi type="italic">Oreb</hi> signifies a <hi type="italic">raven,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zeeb</hi> a <hi type="italic">wolf</hi> (<hi type="italic">corvus</hi> and <hi type="italic">lupus</hi>). These in their flight had taken shelter, one <hi type="italic">in a rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>), the other by a <hi type="italic">wine-press,</hi> as Gideon for fear of them had lately hid his corn by a wine-press, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.11">ch. vi. 11</reference>. But the places of their shelter were made the places of their slaughter, and the memory of it was preserved to posterity in the names of the places, to their perpetual infamy: <hi type="italic">Here fell the princes of Midian.</hi>  <chapter eID="Judg.7"/> <div eID="gen4796" type="x-p"/>

entries.c0cd845a6b72037b27b0a15630a7603835d678d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2280"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.7.1-Judg.7.8">Jud 7:1-8</reference>. Gideon's Army.</title> <div sID="gen3077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2280"/><hi type="bold">1. Jerubbaal--</hi>This had now become Gideon's honorable surname, "the enemy of Baal."<div eID="gen3077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">well--</hi>rather "spring of Harod," that is, "fear, trembling"; probably the same as the fountain in Jezreel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>). It was situated not far from Gilboa, on the confines of Manasseh, and the name "Harod" was bestowed on it with evident reference to the panic which seized the majority of Gideon's troops. The host of the Midianites were on the northern side of the valley, seemingly deeper down in the descent towards the Jordan, near a little eminence. <div eID="gen3078" type="x-p"/>
entries.5885e743882fb213300490e0690fa648a826d634: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2281"/><div sID="gen3079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2281"/><hi type="bold">2. the Lord said unto Gideon, The people ... are too many--</hi>Although the Israelitish army mustered only thirty-two thousand (or one-sixth of the Midianitish host), the number was too great, for it was the Lord's purpose to teach Israel a memorable lesson of dependence on Him. <div eID="gen3079" type="x-p"/>
entries.457c709288c1f143a32c7ce32a3cf01a11f61279: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2282"/><div sID="gen3080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2282"/><hi type="bold">3. Now therefore ..., proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful ... let him return--</hi>This proclamation was in terms of an established law (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.8">De 20:8</reference>). <div eID="gen3080" type="x-p"/>
entries.c09388abdf96bd55663f8951a0f3a7645fd48368: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2283"/><div sID="gen3081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2283"/><hi type="bold">4. too many--</hi>Two reductions were ordered, the last by the application of a test which was made known to Gideon alone. <div eID="gen3081" type="x-p"/>
entries.1876d6220b4d24e4a456102ecaf32bc77f175e0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2284"/><div sID="gen3082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2284"/><hi type="bold">5. bring them down unto the water--</hi>When the wandering people in Asia, on a journey or in haste, come to water, they do not stoop down with deliberation on their knees, but only bend forward as much as is necessary to bring their hand in contact with the stream, and throw it up with rapidity, and at the same time such address, that they do not drop a particle. The Israelites, it seems, were acquainted with the practice; and those who adopted it on this occasion were selected as fit for a work that required expedition. The rest were dismissed according to the divine direction. <div eID="gen3082" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a56cfc55d88fc3604a91c6235272a2def00622d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2285"/><div sID="gen3083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2285"/><hi type="bold">7. the Lord said, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you--</hi>It is scarcely possible to conceive a more severe trial than the command to attack the overwhelming forces of the enemy with such a handful of followers. But Gideon's faith in the divine assurance of victory was steadfast, and it is for this he is so highly commended (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.32">He 11:32</reference>). <div eID="gen3083" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba753790a103f8de63c801f98bc47be226bba9d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2286"/><div sID="gen3084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2286"/><hi type="bold">8. the host of Midian was beneath him in the valley--</hi>Attention to the relative position of the parties is of the greatest importance to an understanding of what follows. <div eID="gen3084" type="x-p"/>
entries.d376516f717393bddeda81cd33363f9a5ed9a180: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2287"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.7.9-Judg.7.15">Jud 7:9-15</reference>. He Is Encouraged by the Dream and the Interpretation of the Barley Cake.</title> <div sID="gen3085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2287"/><hi type="bold">9-10. Arise, get thee down unto the host ... But if thou fear to go down, go thou with Phurah thy servant--</hi>In ancient times it was reckoned no degradation for persons of the highest rank and character to act as spies on an enemy's camp; and so Gideon did on this occasion. But the secret errand was directed by God, who intended that he should hear something which might animate his own valor and that of his troops. <div eID="gen3085" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f3d0d782ffc9f53d317fa3702c181afe5df108d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2288"/><div sID="gen3086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2288"/><hi type="bold">11. the outside of the armed men that were in the host--</hi>"Armed," means embodied under the five officers established by the ordinary laws and usages of encampments. The camp seems to have been unprotected by any rampart, since Gideon had no difficulty in reaching and overhearing a conversation, so important to him. <div eID="gen3086" type="x-p"/>
entries.18b8eec48e39282e8c287fc0ea95cb682f66e704: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2289"/><div sID="gen3087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2289"/><hi type="bold">12. the Midianites and the Amalekites ... lay along in the valley like grasshoppers for multitude; and their camels were without number--</hi>a most graphic description of an Arab encampment. They lay wrapt in sleep, or resting from their day's plunder, while their innumerable camels were stretched round about them. <div eID="gen3087" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f24709b6606b2f8cab059cf453073ec22aa35c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2290"/><div sID="gen3088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2290"/><hi type="bold">13. I dreamed a dream, and, lo, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian--</hi>This was a characteristic and very expressive dream for an Arab in the circumstances. The rolling down the hill, striking against the tents, and overturning them, naturally enough connected it in his mind with the position and meditated attack of the Israelitish leader. The circumstance of the cake, too, was very significant. Barley was usually the food of the poor, and of beasts; but most probably, from the widespread destruction of the crops by the invaders, multitudes must have been reduced to poor and scanty fare. <div eID="gen3088" type="x-p"/>
entries.a53fea71fd06a31730e01e6cc3b5e9c22975d8ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2291"/><div sID="gen3089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2291"/><hi type="bold">15. when Gideon heard the telling of the dream, and the interpretation ... he worshipped--</hi>The incident originated in the secret overruling providence of God, and Gideon, from his expression of pious gratitude, regarded it as such. On his mind, as well as that of his followers, it produced the intended effect--that of imparting new animation and impulse to their patriotism. <div eID="gen3089" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fc70303946e87283f28cb03634f93d1c5c2fe45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2292"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.7.16-Judg.7.24">Jud 7:16-24</reference>. His Stratagem against Midian.</title> <div sID="gen3090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2292"/><hi type="bold">16-22. he divided the three hundred men into three companies--</hi>The object of dividing his forces was, that they might seem to be surrounding the enemy. The pitchers were empty to conceal the torches, and made of earthenware, so as to be easily broken; and the sudden blaze of the held-up lights--the loud echo of the trumpets, and the shouts of Israel, always terrifying (<reference osisRef="Num.23.21">Nu 23:21</reference>), and now more terrible than ever by the use of such striking words, broke through the stillness of the midnight air. The sleepers started from their rest; not a blow was dealt by the Israelites; but the enemy ran tumultuously, uttering the wild, discordant cries peculiar to the Arab race. They fought indiscriminately, not knowing friend from foe. The panic being universal, they soon precipitately fled, directing their flight down to the Jordan, by the foot of the mountains of Ephraim, to places known as the "house of the acacia" [Beth-shittah], and "the meadow of the dance" [Abel-meholah]. <div eID="gen3090" type="x-p"/>
entries.ace428f9ac66f5bb9931996b2ea444b6c687039d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2293"/><div sID="gen3091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2293"/><hi type="bold">23. the men of Israel gathered themselves together--</hi>These were evidently the parties dismissed, who having lingered at a little distance from the scene of contest, now eagerly joined in the pursuit southwestward through the valley. <div eID="gen3091" type="x-p"/>
entries.f17950e58893feef4be6841641cafc63760fd7e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2294"/><div sID="gen3092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2294"/><hi type="bold">24-25. Gideon sent messengers throughout all mount Ephraim--</hi>The Ephraimites lay on the south and could render seasonable aid.<div eID="gen3092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Come ... take before them the waters unto Beth-barah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Judg.3.28">Jud 3:28</reference>). These were the northern fords of the Jordan, to the east-northeast of wady Maleh.<div eID="gen3093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together ... unto Beth-barah--</hi>A <hi type="bold">new conflict ensued, in which two secondary chiefs were seized and slain on the spots where they were respectively taken. The spots were named after these chiefs, Oreb, "the Raven," and Zeeb, "the Wolf"--</hi>appropriate designations of Arab leaders. <chapter eID="Judg.7"/>

entries.25ab9297717502130cc010fc1f303b857fad7a74: <div eID="gen8593" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8594" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8595" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8595" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8594" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8596" type="x-p"/> The Lord commands Gideon to make a selection of a small number of his men to go against the Midianites. Three hundred only are selected; and into the hands of these God promises to deliver the whole Midianitish host, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.1-Jdg.7.8">Jdg 7:1-8</reference>. Gideon is directed to go down unto the host in the night, that he may be encouraged on hearing what they say, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.9-Jdg.7.12">Jdg 7:9-12</reference>. He obeys, and hears a Midianite tell a remarkable dream unto his fellow, which predicted the success of his attack, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.13-Jdg.7.15">Jdg 7:13-15</reference>. He takes encouragement, divides his men into three companies, and gives each a trumpet with a lighted lamp concealed in a pitcher, with directions how to use them, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.16-Jdg.7.18">Jdg 7:16-18</reference>. They come to the Midianitish camp at night, when all suddenly blowing their trumpets and exposing their lamps, the Midianites are thrown into confusion, fly, and are stopped by the Ephraimites at the passage of Jordan, and slain, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.19-Jdg.7.24">Jdg 7:19-24</reference>. Oreb and Zeeb, two Midianitish princes, are slain, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.25">Jdg 7:25</reference>. <div eID="gen8596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8597" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8598" type="x-p"/> Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon - It appears that Jerubbaal was now a surname of Gideon, from the circumstance mentioned <reference osisRef="Jdg.6.32">Jdg 6:32</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.35">Jdg 8:35</reference>. <div eID="gen8598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8599" type="x-p"/> The well of Harod - If this was a town or village, it is nowhere else mentioned. Probably, as חרד charad signifies to shake or tremble through fear, the fountain in question may have had its name from the terror and panic with which the Midianitish host was seized at this place.
entries.6611641086ffb04602fe7969642767ac039bec1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen8599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8600" type="x-p"/> The people that are with thee are too many - Had he led up a numerous host against his enemies, the excellence of the power by which they were discomfited might have appeared to be of man and not of God. By the manner in which this whole transaction was conducted, both the Israelites and Midianites must see that the thing was of God. This would inspire the Israelites with confidence, and the Midianites with fear.
entries.1877718742dd54abbac71c9355339ded001bec3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8601" type="x-p"/> Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return - from Mount Gilead - Gideon was certainly not at Mount Gilead at this time, but rather near Mount Gilboa. Gilead was on the other side of Jordan. Calmet thinks there must either have been two Gileads, which does not from the Scripture appear to be the case, or that the Hebrew text is here corrupted, and that for Gilead we should read Gilboa. This reading, though adopted by Houbigant, is not countenanced by any MS., nor by any of the versions. Dr. Hales endeavors to reconcile the whole, by the supposition that there were in Gideon's army many of the eastern Manassites, who came from Mount Gilead; and that these probably were more afraid of their neighbors, the Midianites, than the western tribes were; and therefore proposes to read the text thus: Whosoever from Mount Gilead is fearful and afraid, let him return (home) and depart early. So there returned (home) twenty-two thousand of the people. Perhaps this is on the whole the best method of solving this difficulty. <div eID="gen8601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8602" type="x-p"/> There returned of the people twenty and two thousand - Gideon's army was at this time thirty-two thousand strong, and after the above address twenty-two thousand went away. How astonishing, that in thirty-two thousand men there should be found not less than twenty-two thousand poltroons, who would neither fight for God nor their oppressed country! A state of slavery debases the mind of man, and renders it incapable of being influenced by the pure principles of patriotism or religion. In behalf of the army of Gideon we may say, if the best appointed armies in Europe had the same address, bona fide, from their generals as the Israelites had, at least an equal proportion would return home.
entries.83aedfce5029beadfa720a93cf3d2c8f46a0bf26: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8603" type="x-p"/> Every one that lappeth of the water - as a dog - The original word ילק yalok is precisely the sound which a dog makes when he is drinking.
entries.ea5751b362fce1f7fa795dda20ad908d6beca454: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8604" type="x-p"/> The number of them that lapped - From this account it appears that some of the people went down on their knees, and putting their mouths to the water, sucked up what they needed; the others stooped down, and taking up water in the hollow of their hands, applied it to their mouth.
entries.0c0029b267a41096974f256cce3611daaf0100d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen8604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8605" type="x-p"/> So the people took victuals - The three hundred men that he reserved took the victuals necessary for the day's expenditure, while the others were dismissed to their tents and their houses as they thought proper.
entries.ce86c8056e949900bd55701792e7a740fc31fc8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen8605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8606" type="x-p"/> I have delivered it into thine hand - I have determined to do it, and it is as sure as if it were done.
entries.1dff77513e9cdd169c05a97ca7582adc99e4e32b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8607" type="x-p"/> Unto the outside of the armed men - No doubt the vast multitudes of Midianites, etc., which came merely for plunder, were wholly unarmed; but they had a guard of armed men, as all the caravans have, and those guards were on the outside of the multitudes; it was to these that Gideon and his servant came.
entries.60023ca52a5ceaa5921b95628e7e4a79c3595326: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen8607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8608" type="x-p"/> Told a dream - Both the dream and the interpretation were inspired by God for the purpose of increasing the confidence of Gideon, and appalling his enemies.
entries.c3fc70f8be2c1f5df754fc9019cc3f5adf5738b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8609" type="x-p"/> Into his hand hath God delivered Midian - This is a full proof that God had inspired both the dream and its interpretation.
entries.7cf39ebb4568c2b72197e06e0c5da92ee5750296: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen8609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8610" type="x-p"/> He divided the three hundred men - Though the victory was to be from the Lord, yet he knew that he ought to use prudential means; and those which he employed on this occasion were the best calculated to answer the end. If he had not used these means, it is not likely that God would have delivered the Midianites into his hands. Sometimes, even in working a miracle, God will have natural means used: Go, dip thyself seven times in Jordan. Go, wash in the pool Siloam.
entries.da89bc026e53f51048dd7fcd02be8833bff700f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen8610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8611" type="x-p"/> The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon - The word חרב chereb, "sword," is not found in this verse, though it is necessarily implied, and is found in <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.20">Jdg 7:20</reference>. But it is found in this place in the Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic, and in eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. The reading appears to be genuine.
entries.3971ca40c4eb6f45a5499b70896f6d52851b9d98: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen8611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8612" type="x-p"/> Blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers - How astonishing must the effect be, in a dark night, of the sudden glare of three hundred torches, darting their splendor, in the same instant, on the half-awakened eyes of the terrified Midianites, accompanied with the clangour of three hundred trumpets, alternately mingled with the thundering shout of חרב ליהוה ולגדעון chereb layhovah ulegidon, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" Origen, in his ninth homily on this book, makes these three hundred men types of the preachers of the Gospel; their trumpets of the preaching of Christ crucified; and their lights or torches, of the holy conduct of righteous men. In some verses of an ancient author, attributed to Tertullian, and written against the heretic Marcion, Gideon's three hundred men are represented as horsemen; and in this number he finds the mystery of the cross; because the Greek letter Τ, tau, which is the numeral for 300, is itself the sign of the cross. The verses, which may be found in vol. v. of the Pisaurian Collection of the Latin heathen and Christian poets, Advers, Marcion., lib. 3, ver. 18, as being very curious, and not often to be met with, I shall here subjoin: - <div eID="gen8612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8613" type="x-p"/> Ex quibus ut Gideon dux agminis, acer in hostem, <div eID="gen8613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8614" type="x-p"/> Non virtute sua tutelam acquirere genti <div eID="gen8614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8615" type="x-p"/> Firmatusque fide signum petit excita menti, <div eID="gen8615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8616" type="x-p"/> Quo vel non posset, vel posset vincere bellum, <div eID="gen8616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8617" type="x-p"/> Vellus ut in noctem positum de rore maderet, <div eID="gen8617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8618" type="x-p"/> Et tellus omnis circum siccata jaceret, <div eID="gen8618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8619" type="x-p"/> Hoc inimicorum palmam coalescere mundo; <div eID="gen8619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8620" type="x-p"/> Atque iterum solo remanenti vellere sicco, <div eID="gen8620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8621" type="x-p"/> Hoc eadem tellus roraret nocte liquore, <div eID="gen8621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8622" type="x-p"/> Hoc etenim signo praedonum stravit acervos. <div eID="gen8622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8623" type="x-p"/> Congressus populo Christi, sine milite multo: <div eID="gen8623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8624" type="x-p"/> Tercenteno equite (numerus Tau littera Graeca) <div eID="gen8624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8625" type="x-p"/> Armatis facibusque et cornibus ore canentum. <div eID="gen8625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8626" type="x-p"/> Vellus erat populus ovium de semine sancto. <div eID="gen8626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8627" type="x-p"/> Nam tellus variae gentes fusaeque per orbem, <div eID="gen8627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8628" type="x-p"/> Verbum quod nutrit, sed nox est mortis imago. <div eID="gen8628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8629" type="x-p"/> Tau signum crucis et cornu praeconia vitae, <div eID="gen8629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8630" type="x-p"/> Lucentesque faces in lychno spiritus ardens. "Gideon, keen in arms, was captain of the host, <div eID="gen8630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8631" type="x-p"/> And acquired redemption for his people, but not by his own power. <div eID="gen8631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8632" type="x-p"/> Being strengthened in faith, his heart was influenced to ask a sign <div eID="gen8632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8633" type="x-p"/> By which he might know whether or not he should be successful in battle. <div eID="gen8633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8634" type="x-p"/> A fleece was so placed by night, that it might be wet with dew; <div eID="gen8634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8635" type="x-p"/> And all the surrounding earth remain dry. <div eID="gen8635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8636" type="x-p"/> By this he was to learn that he should gain the victory over his enemies. <div eID="gen8636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8637" type="x-p"/> The sign was reversed; the fleece remaining dry while all the ground was moist; <div eID="gen8637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8638" type="x-p"/> And by this sign he was to know that he should slaughter those troops of robbers. <div eID="gen8638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8639" type="x-p"/> The people of Christ conquer without any military force; <div eID="gen8639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8640" type="x-p"/> Three hundred horsemen, (for the Greek letter T, tau, is the emblem of the number), <div eID="gen8640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8641" type="x-p"/> Armed with torches, and blowing with trumpets. <div eID="gen8641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8642" type="x-p"/> The fleece of the sheep are the people sprung from the Messiah, <div eID="gen8642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8643" type="x-p"/> And the earth are the various nations dispersed over the world. <div eID="gen8643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> It is the word which nourishes; but might is the image of death. <div eID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8645" type="x-p"/> Tau is the sign of the cross; and the trumpets, the emblems of the heralds of life; <div eID="gen8645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8646" type="x-p"/> And the burning torches in the pitchers, the emblems of the Holy Spirit." <div eID="gen8646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8647" type="x-p"/> We see here what abstruse meanings a strong imagination, assisted by a little piety, may extract from what was never intended to be understood as a mystery.
entries.e2caaf30eaa6432e754268a6eda7c4986dc26c04: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8648" type="x-p"/> They stood every man in his place - Each of the three companies kept its station, and continued to sound their trumpets. The Midianites seeing this, and believing that they were the trumpets of a numerous army which had then penetrated their camp, were thrown instantly into confusion; and supposing that their enemies were in the midst of them, they turned their swords against every man they met, while at the same time they endeavored to escape for their lives. No stratagem was ever better imagined, better executed, or more completely successful.
entries.e10bcfb16ac44ca15c7fc30cc6ca9e396ec3d6e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen8648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> Fled to Beth-shittah - This is no where else mentioned in Scripture. <div eID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> Zererath - This and Tabbath are nowhere else to be found. <div eID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> Abel-meholah - This was the birth-place of the prophet Elisha, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.16">1Kgs 19:16</reference>. It was beyond Jordan, in the tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.12">1Kgs 4:12</reference>. The Zartanah, mentioned in this last quoted verse, was probably the same as Zererath. Its situation corresponds well with Abel-meholah.
entries.50b214c40883b70d7f40cda4101b4fdab8c4e819: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8652" type="x-p"/> The men of Israel gathered - It is very likely that these were some persons whom Gideon had sent home the day before, who now hearing that the Midianites were routed, went immediately in pursuit.
entries.a473d9572baf68ae5b3b72b6f9fe8e6a07591c09: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen8652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8653" type="x-p"/> Take before them the waters unto Beth-barah - This is probably the same place as that mentioned <reference osisRef="Joh.1.28">Joh 1:28</reference>, where the Hebrews forded Jordan under the direction of Joshua. To this place the Midianites directed their flight that they might escape into their own country; and here, being met by the Ephraimites, they appear to have been totally overthrown, and their two generals taken.
entries.ba66d7cf65aa72cde0f5f6d6f41a2b2df0174ad1: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen8653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> They slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb - These two generals had taken shelter, one in the cavern of the rock, the other in the vat of a winepress; both of which places were from this circumstance, afterwards called by their names. <div eID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8655" type="x-p"/> Brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon - Oreb signifies a raven and Zeeb a wolf. In all ancient nations we find generals and princes taking their names from both birds and beasts; the Romans had their Gracchi, jackdaws; Corvini, crows; Aquilini, eagles, etc. We have the same in our Crows, Wolfs, Lyons, Hawkes, Bulls, Kidds, etc. Among barbarous nations the head of the conquered chief was often brought to the conqueror. Pompey's head was brought to Caesar; Cicero's head, to Mark Antony; the heads of Ahab's children, to Jehu, etc. These barbarities are not often practiced now, except among the Mohammedans or the savages of Africa and America; and for the credit of human nature it is a pity that such barbarous atrocities had ever been committed.  <chapter eID="Judg.7"/> <div eID="gen8655" type="x-p"/>

entries.7fdcfd0e0592452e0e034d2fc2b2f6c6487ef83e: Mustering of the Army that Gideon had Collected. - Jdg 7:1. When Gideon had been assured of the help of God by this double sign, he went to the battle early the next morning with the people that he had gathered around him. The Israelites encamped above the fountain of <hi type="italic">Harod</hi>, i.e., upon a height at the foot of which this fountain sprang; but the camp of Midian was to him (Gideon) to the north of the hill <hi type="italic">Moreh</hi> in the valley (of Jezreel: see Jdg 6:33). The geographical situation of these two places cannot be determined with certainty. The fountain of <hi type="italic">Harod</hi> is never mentioned again, though there is a place of that name referred to in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.25">2Sa 23:25</reference> as the home of two of David’s heroes; and it was from this, no doubt, that the fountain was named. The hill <hi type="italic">Moreh</hi> is also unknown. As it was by the valley (of Jezreel), we cannot possibly think of the grove of <hi type="italic">Moreh</hi> at Shechem (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.30">Deu 11:30</reference>).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> endeavours to settle the position of the place from our knowledge of the country, which is for the most part definite enough. Starting with the assumption that the fountain of <hi type="italic">Harod</hi> cannot be any other than the “fountain in Jezreel” mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>, where Saul and the Israelites encamped at Gilboa (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.4">1Sa 28:4</reference>) to fight against the Philistines who were posted at <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi>, a place on the western slope of the so-called Little Hermon, he concludes that the fountain of <hi type="italic">Harod</hi> must be the present <hi type="italic">Ain Jalud</hi>, and the hill of <hi type="italic">Moreh</hi> the Little <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi> itself. These combinations are certainly possible, for we have nothing definite to oppose to them; still they are very uncertain, as they simply rest upon the very doubtful assumption that the only fountain in the plain of Jezreel was the celebrated fountain called <hi type="italic">Ain Jalud</hi>, and are hardly reconcilable with the account given of the route which was taken by the defeated Midianites (Jdg 7:25. and Jdg 8:4).</note>
entries.f980776749c4131adce0f8e4db1fc54f6b6b3caf: Jdg 7:2-3 <div eID="gen3258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3259" type="x-p"/> The army of the Israelites amounted to 32,000 men (Jdg 7:4), but that of the Midianites and their allies was about 135,000 (Jdg 8:10), so that they were greatly superior to the Israelites in numbers. Nevertheless the Lord said to Gideon, “<hi type="italic">The people that are with thee are too many for me to give Midian into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, My hand hath helped me.</hi>” רב followed by מן is to be understood as a comparative. Gideon was therefore to have a proclamation made before all the people: “<hi type="italic">Whosoever is fearful and despondent, let him turn and go back from Mount Gilead.</hi>” The ἁπ. λεγ. צפר, judging from the Arabic, which signifies to plait, viz., hair, ropes, etc., and the noun צפירה, a circle or circuitous orbit, probably signifies to twist one’s self round; hence in this instance to return in windings, to slink away in bypaths. The expression “<hi type="italic">from Mount Gilead</hi>,” however, is very obscure. The mountain (or the mountains) of Gilead was on the eastern side of the Jordan; but the Israelitish army was encamped in or near the plain of Jezreel, in the country to the west of the Jordan, and had been gathered from the western tribes alone; so that even the inadmissible rendering, Let him turn and go home to the mountains of Gilead, would not give any appropriate sense. The only course left therefore is either to pronounce it an error of the text, as <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> have done, and to regard “Gilead” as a mistake for “Gilboa,” or to conclude that there was also a mountain or mountain range named <hi type="italic">Gilead</hi> by the plain of Jezreel in western Palestine, just as, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>, there was a mountain, or range of mountains, called <hi type="italic">Seir</hi>, in the territory of Judah, of which nothing further is known. The appeal which Gideon is here directed to make to the army was prescribed in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.8">Deu 20:8</reference>) for every war in which the Israelites should be engaged, and its general object was to fortify the spirit of the army be removing the cowardly and desponding. But in the case before us the intention of the Lord was to deprive His people of all ground for self-glorification. Hence the result of the appeal was one which Gideon himself certainly did not expect, - namely, that more than two-thirds of the soldiers gathered round him - 22,000 men of the people - turned back, and only 10,000 remained.
entries.7c618c46174f3bc203d33fa7633cf81683a2675a: Jdg 7:4 <div eID="gen3259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3260" type="x-p"/> But even this number was regarded by the Lord as still too great, so that He gave to Gideon the still further command, “<hi type="italic">Bring them</hi> (the 10,000 men) <hi type="italic">down to the water</hi>,” i.e., the waters formed from the fountain of Harod, “<hi type="italic">and I will purify them for thee there </hi>(צרף, separate those appointed for the battle from the rest of the army; the singular suffix refers to העם), <hi type="italic">and say to thee, This shall go with thee, and that,</hi>” i.e., show thee each individual who is to go with thee to the battle, and who not.
entries.66e5b3cf05a5902a7ab7eac0e67daef07445a183: Jdg 7:5-6 <div eID="gen3260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3261" type="x-p"/> Gideon was to divide the people by putting all those who should lick the water with their tongue as a dog licketh into one class, and all those who knelt down to drink into another, and so separating the latter from the former. The number of those who licked the water into their mouth with their hand amounted to 300, and all the rest knelt down to drink. “<hi type="italic">To lick with their hand to their mouth,</hi>” i.e., to take the water from the brook with the hollow of their hand, and lap it into the mouth with their tongue as a dog does, is only a more distinct expression for “licking with the tongue.” The 300 men who quenched their thirst in this manner were certainly not the cowardly or indolent who did not kneel down to drink in the ordinary way, either from indolence or fear, as <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi>, <hi type="italic">Theodoret</hi>, and others supposed, but rather the bravest-namely those who, when they reached a brook before the battle, did not allow themselves time to kneel down and satisfy their thirst in the most convenient manner, but simply took up some water with their hands as they stood in their military accoutrements, to strengthen themselves for the battle, and then proceeded without delay against the foe. By such a sign as this, <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> supposes that even an ordinary general might have been able to recognise the bravest of his army. No doubt: but if this account had not been handed down, it is certain that it would never have occurred to an ordinary or even a distinguished general to adopt such a method of putting the bravery of his troops to the test; and even Gideon, the hero of God, would never have thought of diminishing still further through such a trial an army which had already become so small, or of attempting to defeat an army of more than 100,000 men by a few hundred of the bravest men, if the Lord himself had not commanded it. <div eID="gen3261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3262" type="x-p"/> Whilst the Lord was willing to strengthen the feeble faith of Gideon by the sign with the fleece of wool, and thus to raise him up to full confidence in the divine omnipotence, He also required of him, when thus strengthened, an attestation of his faith, by the purification of his army that he might give the whole glory to Him, and accept the victory over that great multitude from His hand alone.
entries.489b58918b2be2b1e10b9a8f1b0d0dcfe1a6c61a: Jdg 7:7 <div eID="gen3262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3263" type="x-p"/> After his fighting men had been divided into a small handful of 300 men on the one hand, and the large host of 9700 on the other, by the fulfilment of the command of God, the Lord required of him that he should send away the latter, “every man to his place,” i.e., to his own home, promising that He would save Israel by the 300 men, and deliver the Midianites into their hand. The promise preceded the command, to render it easier to Gideon to obey it. “<hi type="italic">All the people</hi>,” after taking out the 300 men, that is to say, the 9700 that remained.
entries.c11733bd004c78499b56a863cd1f10288392c664: Jdg 7:8 <div eID="gen3263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3264" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">So they</hi> (the 300 picked men) <hi type="italic">took the provision of the people in their hand, and</hi> <hi type="italic">their</hi> (the people’s) <hi type="italic">trumpets</hi> (the suffix points back to העם, the people); <hi type="italic">and all the men of Israel </hi>(the 9700) <hi type="italic">he had sent away every one to his tents,</hi> i.e., to his home (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.16.7">Deu 16:7</reference>), <hi type="italic">and the three hundred men he had kept by himself; but the camp of the Midianites was below to him in the valley.</hi>” These words bring the preparations for the battle to a close, and the last clause introduces the ensuing conflict and victory. In the first clause העם (the people) cannot be the subject, partly because of the actual sense, since the 300 warriors, who are no doubt the persons intended (cf. Jdg 7:16), cannot be called “the people,” in distinction from “all the men of Israel,” and partly also because of the expression את־צדה, which would be construed in that case without any article in violation of the ordinary rule. We must rather read העם את־צדת, as the lxx and the Chaldee have done. The 300 men took the provision of the people, i.e., provision for the war, from the people who had been sent away, and the war-trumpets; so that every one of the 300 had a trumpet now, and as the provision of the people was also probably kept in vessels or pitchers (<hi type="italic">caddim</hi>: Jdg 7:16), a jug as well. The subject to יקחוּ is to be taken from the first clause of the seventh verse. The sentences which follow from כּל־אישׁ ואת are circumstantial clauses, introduced to bring out distinctly the situation in which Gideon was now placed. בּ החזיק, the opposite of שׁלּח, to send away, signifies to hold fast, to keep back or by himself, as in Exo 9:2. לו, to him, Gideon, who was standing by the fountain of Harod with his 300 men, the situation of Midian was underneath in the valley (see Jdg 7:1, and Jdg 6:33).
entries.1bfb839fdc2b68a877a1f39b85e727004a10e472: Jdg 7:9-10 <div eID="gen3264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3265" type="x-p"/> Gideon’s Battle and Victory. - <hi type="italic">Jdg 7:9-11</hi>. The following night the Lord commanded Gideon to go down to the camp of the enemy, as He had given it into his hand (the perfect is used to denote the purpose of God which had already been formed, as in Jdg 4:14).
