But in order to fill him with confidence for such an enterprise, which to all human appearance was a very rash one, God added, “<hi type="italic">If thou art afraid to go down, go thou with thine attendant Purah down to the camp, and thou wilt hear what they say, and thy hands will thereby become strong.</hi>” The meaning of the protasis is not, If thou art afraid to go down into the camp of the enemy alone, or to visit the enemy unarmed, take Purah thine armour-bearer with thee, to make sure that thou hast weapons to use (<hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>); for, apart from the fact that the addition “unarmed” is perfectly arbitrary, the apodosis “thou wilt see,” etc., by no means agrees with this explanation. The meaning is rather this: Go with thy 300 men into (בּ) the hostile camp to smite it, for I have given it into thy hand; but if thou art afraid to do this, go down with thine attendant to (אל) the camp, to ascertain the state and feeling of the foe, and thou wilt hear what they say, i.e., as we gather from what follows, how they are discouraged, have lost all hope of defeating you, and from that thou wilt gather courage and strength for the battle. On the expression “<hi type="italic">thine hands shall be strengthened,</hi>” see 2Sa 2:7. The expression which follows, בּמּחנה וירדתּ, is not a mere repetition of the command to go down with his attendant to the hostile camp, but describes the result of the stimulus given to his courage: And then thou wilt go fearlessly into the hostile camp to attack the foe. בּמּחנה ירד (Jdg 7:9, Jdg 7:11) is to be distinguished from המּחנה ירד in Jdg 7:10. The former signifies to go down into the camp to smite the foe; the latter, to go down to the camp to reconnoitre it, and is equivalent to the following clause: “he went to the outside of the camp.”
entries.21205c4740302a830320c145bbd956263f6fa396: Jdg 7:11-14 <div eID="gen3265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3266" type="x-p"/> But when Gideon came with his attendant to the end of the armed men (<hi type="italic">chamushim</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.1.14">Jos 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">Exo 13:18</reference>) in the hostile camp, and the enemy were lying spread out with their camels in the valley, an innumerable multitude, he heard one (of the fighting men) relate to his fellow (i.e., to another) a dream which he had had: “<hi type="italic">Behold a cake of barley bread was rolling into the camp of Midian, and it came to the tent and smote it, so that it fell and turned upwards, and let the tent lay along.</hi>” Then the other replied, “<hi type="italic">This is nothing else than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash the Israelite: God hath given Midian and all the camp into his hand.</hi>” “The end of fighting men” signifies the outermost or foremost of the outposts in the enemy’s camp, which contained not only fighting men, but the whole of the baggage of the enemy, who had invaded the land as nomads, with their wives, their children, and their flocks. In Jdg 7:12, the innumerable multitude of the enemy is described once more in the form of a circumstantial clause, as in Jdg 6:5, not so much to distinguish the fighting men from the camp generally, as to bring out more vividly the contents and meaning of the following dream. The comparison of the enemy to the sand by the sea-side recalls <reference osisRef="Josh.11.4">Jos 11:4</reference>, and is frequently met with (see <reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.13">Gen 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.5">1Sa 13:5</reference>). With the word ויּבא in Jdg 7:13, the thread of the narrative, which was broken off by the circumstantial clause in Jdg 7:12, is resumed and carried further. The ἁπ. λεγ. צלוּל (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, צליל) is rendered <hi type="italic">cake</hi>, <hi type="italic">placenta</hi>, by the early translators: see <hi type="italic">Ges</hi>. Thes. p. 1170. The derivation of the word has been disputed, and is by no means certain, as צלל does not give any suitable meaning, either in the sense of to ring or to be overshadowed, and the meaning to roll (<hi type="italic">Ges. l.c</hi>.) cannot be philologically sustained; whilst צלה, to roast, can hardly be thought of, since this is merely used to denote the roasting of flesh, and קלה was the word commonly applied to the roasting of grains, and even “the roasted of barley bread” would hardly be equivalent to <hi type="italic">subcinericeus panis ex hordeo</hi> (<hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>). “<hi type="italic">The tent</hi>,” with the definite article, is probably the principal tent in the camp, i.e., the tent of the general. למעלה, upwards, so that the bottom came to the top. “<hi type="italic">The tent lay along</hi>,” or the tent fell, lay in ruins, is added to give emphasis to the words. “<hi type="italic">This is nothing if not</hi>,” i.e., nothing but. The cake of bread which had rolled into the Midianitish camp and overturned the tent, signifies nothing else than the sword of Gideon, i.e., Gideon, who is bursting into the camp with his sword, and utterly destroying it. <div eID="gen3266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3267" type="x-p"/> This interpretation of the dream was certainly a natural one under the circumstances. Gideon is especially mentioned simply as the leader of the Israelites; whilst the loaf of barley bread, which was the food of the poorer classes, is to be regarded as strictly speaking the symbol of Israel, which was so despised among the nations. The rising of the Israelites under Gideon had not remained a secret to the Midianites, and no doubt filled them with fear; so that in a dream this fear might easily assume the form of the defeat or desolation and destruction of their camp by Gideon. And the peculiar form of the dream is also psychologically conceivable. As the tent is everything to a nomad, he might very naturally picture the cultivator of the soil as a man whose life is all spent in cultivating and baking bread. In this way bread would become almost involuntarily a symbol of the cultivator of the soil, whilst in his own tent he would see a symbol not only of his mode of life, but of his freedom, greatness, and power. If we add to this, that the free pastoral tribes, particularly the Bedouins of Arabia, look down with pride not only upon the poor tillers of the soil, but even upon the inhabitants of towns, and that in Palestine, the land of wheat, none but the poorer classes feed upon barley bread, we have here all the elements out of which the dream of the Midianitish warrior was formed. The Israelites had really been crushed by the Midianites into a poor nation of slaves. But whilst the dream itself admits of being explained in this manner in a perfectly natural way, it acquires the higher supernatural character of a divine inspiration, from the fact that God not only foreknew it, but really caused the Midianite to dream, and to relate the dream to his comrade, just at the time when Gideon had secretly entered the camp, so that he should hear it, and discover therefrom, as God had foretold him, the despondency of the foe. Under these circumstances, Gideon could not fail to regard the dream as a divine inspiration, and to draw the assurance from it, that God had certainly given the Midianites into his hands.
entries.86773c87233acbb51af7f343f33517dc9a16700d: Jdg 7:15-18 <div eID="gen3267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3268" type="x-p"/> When therefore he had heard the dream related and interpreted, he worshipped, praising the Lord with joy, and returned to the camp to attack the enemy without delay. He then divided the 300 men into three companies, i.e., three attacking columns, and gave them all trumpets and empty pitchers, with torches in the pitchers in their hands. The pitchers were taken that they might hide the burning torches in them during their advance to surround the enemy’s camp, and then increase the noise at the time of the attack, by dashing the pitchers to pieces (Jdg 7:20), and thus through the noise, as well as the sudden lighting up of the burning torches, deceive the enemy as to the strength of the army. At the same time he commanded them, “<hi type="italic">See from me, and do likewise</hi>,” - a short expression for, As ye see me do, so do ye also (כּן, without the previous כּ, or כּאשׁר as in Jdg 5:15; see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §260, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), - “<hi type="italic">I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me; ye also blow the trumpets round about the entire camp,</hi>” which the 300 men divided into three companies were to surround, “<hi type="italic">and say, To the Lord and Gideon</hi>.” According to Jdg 7:20, this war-cry ran fully thus: “<hi type="italic">Sword to</hi> (for) <hi type="italic">the Lord and Gideon</hi>.” This addition in Jdg 7:20, however, does not warrant us in inserting “<hi type="italic">chereb</hi>” (sword) in the text here, as some of the early translators and MSS have done.<note placement="foot">Similar stratagems to the one adopted by Gideon here are recorded by <hi type="italic">Polyaenus</hi> (Strateg. ii. c. 37) of Dicetas, at the taking of Heraea, and by <hi type="italic">Plutarch</hi> (<hi type="italic">Fabius Max</hi>. c. 6) of Hannibal, when he was surrounded and completely shut in by Fabius Maximus. An example from modern history is given by <hi type="italic">Niebuhr</hi> (Beschr. von Arabien, p. 304). About the middle of the eighteenth century two Arabian chiefs were fighting for the Imamate of Oman. One of them, Bel-Arab, besieged the other, Achmed ben Said, with four or five thousand men, in a small castle on the mountain. But the latter slipped out of the castle, collected together several hundred men, gave every soldier a sign upon his head, that they might be able to distinguish friends from foes, and sent small companies to all the passes. Every one had a trumpet to blow at a given signal, and thus create a noise at the same time on every side. The whole of the opposing army was thrown in this way into disorder, since they found all the passes occupied, and imagined the hostile army to be as great as the noise.</note>
entries.0d9861eea2586394afdfc3f9ef922d996bb7e6e2: Jdg 7:19 <div eID="gen3268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3269" type="x-p"/> Gideon then proceeded with the 100 who were with him, i.e., the company which was led by himself personally, to the end of the hostile camp, at the beginning of the middle watch, i.e., at midnight ראשׁ is an accusative defining the time: see <hi type="italic">Ges</hi>. 118, 2, and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §204, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The only other watch that is mentioned in the Old Testament beside the middle night-watch, is the morning night-watch (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.11">1Sa 11:11</reference>), from which it has been correctly inferred, that the Israelites divided the night into three night-watches. The division into four watches (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.25">Mat 14:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.48">Mar 6:48</reference>) was first adopted by the Jews from the Romans. “<hi type="italic">They</hi> (the Midianites) <hi type="italic">had</hi> <hi type="italic">only</hi> (just) <hi type="italic">posted the watchmen</hi> (of the middle watch),” - a circumstantial clause, introduced to give greater distinctness to the situation. When the first sentries were relieved, and the second posted, so that they thought they might make quite sure of their night’s rest once more, Gideon and his host arrived at the end of the camp, and, as we must supply from the context, the other two hosts at two other ends of the camp, who all blew their trumpets, breaking the pitchers in their hands at the same time. The <hi type="italic">inf. abs</hi>. נפוץ, as a continuation of the finite verb יתקעוּ, indicates that the fact was contemporaneous with the previous one (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.).
entries.61a229061886f1a8760595647d4a749e1c16a827: Jdg 7:20-21 <div eID="gen3269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> According to the command which they had received (Jdg 7:17), the other two tribes followed his example. “<hi type="italic">Then the three companies blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers, and held the torches in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right to blow, and cried, Sword to the Lord and Gideon! And they stood every one his place round about the camp,</hi>” sc., without moving, so that the Midianites necessarily thought that there must be a numerous army advancing behind the torch-bearers. וגו ויּרץ, “<hi type="italic">and the whole army ran,</hi>” i.e., there began a running hither and thither in the camp of the enemy, who had been frightened out of their night’s rest by the unexpected blast of the trumpets, the noise, and the war-cry of the Israelitish warriors; “<hi type="italic">and they</hi> (the enemy<hi type="italic">) lifted up a cry</hi> (of anguish and alarm), <hi type="italic">and caused to fly</hi>” (carried off), sc., their tents (i.e., their families) and their herds, or all their possessions (cf. Jdg 6:11; <reference osisRef="Exod.9.20">Exo 9:20</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> יניסוּ is the original reading, and the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ינוּסוּ a bad emendation.
entries.3b2cebf97bc2c8f2a7602744f802813b7111b02f: Jdg 7:22 <div eID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3271" type="x-p"/> Whilst the 300 men blew their trumpets, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah set the sword of one against the other, and against the whole camp,</hi>” i.e., caused one to turn his sword against the other and against all the camp, that is to say, not merely man against man, but against every one in the camp, so that there arose a terrible slaughter throughout the whole camp. The first clause, “<hi type="italic">and the three hundred blew the trumpets,</hi>” simply resumes the statement in Jdg 7:20, “the three companies blew the trumpets,” for the purpose of appending to it the further progress of the attack, and the result of the battle. <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> inserts in a very arbitrary manner the words, “the second time.” His explanation of the next clause (“then the 300 fighting men of Gideon drew the sword at Jehovah’s command, every man against his man”) is still more erroneous, since it does violence to the constant usage of the expression בּרעהוּ אישׁ (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">1Sa 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.23">2Ch 20:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Isa 3:5</reference>; Zec 8:10). “<hi type="italic">And all the camp of the Midianites fled to Beth-shittah to Zeredah, to the shore of Abel-meholah, over Tabbath.</hi>” The situation of these places, which are only mentioned here, with the exception of Abel-meholah, the home of Elisha (1Ki 19:16; 1Ki 4:12), has not yet been determined. According to the Syriac, the Arabic, and some of the MSS, we should read <hi type="italic">Zeredathah</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Zererathah</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Zeredathah</hi> is only another form for <hi type="italic">Zarthan</hi> (comp. 1Ki 7:46 with <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.17">2Ch 4:17</reference>). This is favoured by the situation of <hi type="italic">Zarthan</hi> in the valley of the Jordan, probably near the modern <hi type="italic">Kurn</hi> <hi type="italic">Sartabeh</hi> (see p. 35), inasmuch as in all probability Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah are to be sought for in the valley of the Jordan; and according to Jdg 7:24, the enemy fled to the Jordan. <hi type="italic">Beth-shittah</hi>, i.e., acacia-house, is not the same place as the village of <hi type="italic">Shutta</hi> mentioned by <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (iii. p. 219), since this village, according to <hi type="italic">Van de Velde's</hi> map, was to the north of Gilboa. For although <hi type="italic">Shutta</hi> is favoured by the circumstance, that from a very ancient time there was a road running from Jezreel along the valley, between the so-called Little Hermon (Duhy) and the mountains of Gilboa, and past Beisan to the Jordan; and the valley of Jalud, on the northern side of which Shutta was situated, may be regarded as the opening of the plain of Jezreel into the valley of the Jordan (see <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. p. 41, and <hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. iii. p. 176); and <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi> conjectures from this, that “the flight of the Midianites was apparently directed to Bethsean, on account of the nature of the ground,” - this assumption is rendered very questionable by the fact that the flying foe did not cross the Jordan in the neighbourhood of Beisan, but much farther to the south, viz., according to Jdg 8:4, in the neighbourhood of <hi type="italic">Succoth</hi>, which was on the south side of the Nahr Zerka (Jabbok). From this we are led to conjecture, that they were not encamped in the north-eastern part of the plain of Jezreel, in the neighbourhood of Jezreel (Zerin) and Shunem (Solam), but in the south-eastern part of this plain, and that after they had been beaten there they fled southwards from Gilboa, say from the district of Ginaea (Jenin) to the Jordan. In this case we have to seek for Abel-shittah on the south-east of the mountains of Gilboa, to the north of Zeredathah (Zarthan). From this point they fled on still farther to the “<hi type="italic">shore of Abel-meholah</hi>.” שׂפה does not mean boundary, but brink; here the bank of the Jordan, like היּרדּן שׂפת in 2Ki 2:13. The bank or strand of <hi type="italic">Abel-meholah</hi> is that portion of the western bank of the Jordan or of the Ghor, above which Abel-meholah was situated. According to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> Ἀβελμαελαί, <hi type="italic">Abelmaula</hi>), this place was in the <hi type="italic">Aulon</hi> (or Ghor), ten Roman miles to the south of Scythopolis (Beisan), and was called at that time Βηθμαιελά or <hi type="italic">Bethaula</hi>. According to this statement, <hi type="italic">Abel-meholah</hi> would have to be sought for near <hi type="italic">Churbet</hi> <hi type="italic">es</hi> <hi type="italic">Shuk</hi>, in the neighbourhood of the Wady <hi type="italic">Maleh</hi> (see V. <hi type="italic">de Velde</hi>, Mem. p. 280). And lastly, <hi type="italic">Tabbath</hi> must have been situated somewhere to the south of Abel-meholah.
entries.c2654beced2516f2499d18b0dc346d6c9049f5fb: Jdg 7:23 <hi type="italic">Pursuit of the Enemy as far as the Jordan</hi>. - Jdg 7:23. As soon as the Midianites had been put to flight, the Israelitish men of Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh, let themselves be convened for the purpose of pursuing them: i.e., the men of these tribes, whom Gideon had sent away before the battle, and who were on their way home, could be summoned back again in a very short time to join in the pursuit of the flying foe. The omission of Zebulun (Jdg 6:35) is, in all probability, simply to be attributed to the brevity of the account.
entries.8283a9c1d2e002b6f612b28c2703bf8162c9e2ae: Jdg 7:24-25 <div eID="gen3271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3272" type="x-p"/> In order to cut off the retreat of the enemy who was flying to the Jordan, Gideon sent messengers into the whole of the mountains of Ephraim with this appeal to the Ephraimites, “<hi type="italic">Come down</hi> (from your mountains into the lowlands of the Jordan) <hi type="italic">to meet Midian, and take the waters from them to Bethbarah and the Jordan,</hi>” sc., by taking possession of this district (see Jdg 3:28). “<hi type="italic">The waters</hi>,” mentioned before the Jordan and distinguished from it, must have been streams across which the flying foe would have to cross to reach the Jordan, namely, the different brooks and rivers, such as Wady <hi type="italic">Maleh</hi>, <hi type="italic">Fyadh, Jamel, Tubâs</hi>, etc., which flowed down from the eastern side of the mountains of Ephraim into the Jordan, and ran through the Ghor to Bethbarah. The situation of <hi type="italic">Bethbarah</hi> is unknown. Even <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> could say nothing definite concerning the place; and the conjecture that it is the same as Bethabara, which has been regarded ever since the time of Origen as the place mentioned in Joh 1:28 where John baptized, throws no light upon the subject, as the situation of Bethabara is also unknown, to say nothing of the fact that the identity of the two names is very questionable. The Ephraimites responded to this appeal and took possession of the waters mentioned, before the Midianites, who could only move slowly with their flocks and herds, were able to reach the Jordan. They then captured two of the princes of the Midianites and put them to death: one of them, <hi type="italic">Oreb</hi>, i.e., the raven, at the rock <hi type="italic">Oreb</hi>; the other, <hi type="italic">Zeeb</hi>, i.e., the wolf, at the wine-press of <hi type="italic">Zeeb</hi>. Nothing further is known about these two places. The rock of <hi type="italic">Oreb</hi> is only mentioned again in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Isa 10:26</reference>, when the prophet alludes to this celebrated victory. So much, however, is evident from the verse before us, viz., that the Midianites were beaten by the Ephraimites at both places, and that the two princes fell there, and the places received their names from that circumstance. They were not situated in the land to the east of the Jordan, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Isa 10:26</reference>), <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>, and others infer from the fact that the Ephraimites brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon ליּרדּן מעבר (Jdg 7:25), but on the western side of the Jordan, where the Ephraimites had taken possession of the waters and the Jordan in front of the Midianites. ליּרדּן מעבר does not mean “from the other side of the Jordan,” but simply “<hi type="italic">on the other side of</hi> (beyond) <hi type="italic">the Jordan</hi>,” as in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.32">Jos 13:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.7">Jos 18:7</reference>; 1Ki 14:15; and the statement here is not that the Ephraimites brought the heads from the other side to Gideon on the west of the river, but that they brought them to Gideon when he was in the land to the east of the Jordan. This explanation of the words is required by the context, as well as by the foregoing remark, “they pursued Midian,” according to which the Ephraimites continued the pursuit of the Midianites after slaying these princes, and also by the complaint brought against Gideon by the Ephraimites, which is not mentioned till afterwards (Jdg 8:1.), that he had not summoned them to the war. It is true, this is given before the account of Gideon’s crossing over the Jordan (Jdg 8:4), but in order of time it did not take place till afterwards, and, as <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> has correctly shown, the historical sequence is somewhat anticipated.  <chapter eID="Judg.7"/> <div eID="gen3272" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>THen Jerubbaal (who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Gideon) and all the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, rose up early, and pitched beside the well of Harod: so that the host of the Midianites were on the north-side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> with thee <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> too many for me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> For my purpose; which is, so to deliver <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> that it may appear to be my own miraculous act, that so I may have all the Glory of it, and they may be more strong<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly obliged to love and serve me.</ns0:note> to give the
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:197" />
Midianites into their hand, lest Israel vaunt them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 20. 6.</ns0:note> Whosoever <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not that famous <ns0:hi>Mount Gilead</ns0:hi> which was beyond <ns0:hi>Ior<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>;</ns0:hi> for it is apparent that both the Camps of the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>Midianites</ns0:hi> were on this side <ns0:hi>Iordan:</ns0:hi> but another <ns0:hi>Mount Gilead</ns0:hi> in the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Manasseh;</ns0:hi> which might be so <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>alled, either for some resemblance it had with the other <ns0:hi>Mount Gilead,</ns0:hi> in remembrance of their Father <ns0:hi>Gilead;</ns0:hi> or, that this might be a Memorial of their near relation to their Brethren, notwithstanding their being divided one from another by <ns0:hi>Iordan;</ns0:hi> or, for some other reason now unknown at this <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>istance of Time and Place. Or, the words may be rendred <ns0:hi>towards Mount Gilead;</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Particle, <ns0:hi>min,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>mem,</ns0:hi> is sometimes rendred <ns0:hi>towards,</ns0:hi> of which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 11. 2. and 13. 11. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 2. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. 2. And so it may be understood of the famous <ns0:hi>Mount Gilead,</ns0:hi> beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> which he may mention here, either, 1. Because many of his Soldiers were of that half Tribe of <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi> which dwelt there, and so it was most proper for them to return thither: Or, 2. Because that was their safest course, to get furthest from the danger which they feared; Or, 3. Because though he would remove them from danger, yet he would not have them dispersed, but kept together in a Body about <ns0:hi>Mount Gilead;</ns0:hi> knowing that they who had not Courage enough to Fight their Enemies, might have Va<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And the LORD said unto Gideon, The peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> yet too many: bring them down unto the water <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either that which ran from the Well of <ns0:hi>Harod,</ns0:hi> men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. or some other Brook.</ns0:note>, and I will try them for thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Because thy Proclama<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion hath not sufficiently tried them; for many who are fearful indeed, will put on the face, and desire the opinion of being Valiant Persons; I will take another course.</ns0:note> there, and it shall be, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> of whom I say unto thee, This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee: and of whomsoever I say unto thee, This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go up.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 So he brought down the people unto the wa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter: and the LORD said unto Gideon, every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself, likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">It is true, there may be natural reasons given, why some did onely Lap of the Water, when others bowed down to drink; from the Temperance, or Fortitude, or Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tience, or Strength, or Diligence of the one; and the Intem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perance, or Cowardice, or Impatience, or Weakness, or Slothfulness of the other; but these seem to be meer con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jectures: The true reason and design of this course, seems to be onely this, That God would reduce them to a very small number, which was likely to be done by this means; for the Season of the year being hot, and the generality of the Soldiers weary, and thirsty, and faint, they would most probably bow down upon their Knees, that they might more fully refresh themselves by a liberal draught, as in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed they did; and it could be expected that there would be but few, who either could or would deny themselves in this matter; especially, when God concurred in the work, and so disposed of the Minds and Bodies of them, that all, except Three Hundred, should lye down to drink.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And the number of them that lapped, <ns0:hi>put<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting</ns0:hi> their hand to their mouth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Taking up a little water in the Palm of their Hands to put into their mouths.</ns0:note>, were three hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred men: but all the rest of the people bowed down upon their knees to drink water.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And the LORD said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped, will I save you, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> people go every man unto his place <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And the Midianites, and the Amalekites, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. 5, 33. and 8. 10.</ns0:note> all the children of the east, lay along in the valley like grashoppers for multitude, and their camels <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> without number, as the sand by the sea-side for multitude.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> tumbled into the host of Midian, and came unto a tent, and smote it that it fell, and overturned it, that the tent lay all along.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And his fellow answered and said, This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> nothing else save the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">As there are many examples of significant Dreams, gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven by God to Heathens, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 41. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. and 4. so some of them had the gift of Interpreting Dreams; which they sometimes did by Study and Art, and sometimes by Divine direction in this case.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> into his hand hath God delivered Midian and all his host.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">For though 200 of his men were placed on other sides of the Camp; yet they were so disposed, that some person or persons, set as Watch-men, might see what was done, and give notice to the rest to follow the Example.</ns0:note>; and behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> as I do, so shall ye do.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 When I blow with a trumpet, I, and all that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry side of all the camp, and say, <ns0:hi>The sword</ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> for the LORD and Gideon.</ns0:note> of the LORD, and of Gideon <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He mentions his own Name, together with Gods, not out of vain ostentation or arrogance, as if he would equal himself with God; for he mentions God in the first and chief place, and himself onely as his Minister; but from prudent Policy, because his Name was grown formidable to them, and so was likely to further his Design, and their Fight, as it did.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 ¶ So Gideon, and the hundred men that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, came unto the outside of the camp, in the beginning of the middle watch <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
